query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (approximately 2–5 at.%) of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure in air, thereby improving its oxidation resistance without degrading its intrinsic room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with established room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and yield strength at high temperature (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of aluminum (around 2–5 at.%) during the melting and casting process.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours (similar to conditions in previous oxidation-protection studies) and subsequent mechanical testing to confirm preserved ductility and yield strength.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added Al preferentially oxidizes at high temperature to form a highly stable Al2O3 scale. This alumina layer acts as an effective barrier to further oxygen diffusion, thereby inhibiting internal oxidation (pesting) and protecting the underlying refractory matrix while retaining the alloy's mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic alloy, the Al-alloyed version is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation rate (i.e., reduced mass gain or oxide scale thickness) after 5 hours of air exposure at 800 °C, with mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) remaining within acceptable ranges.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance, leading to rapid oxidation and potential pesting under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature oxidation conditions (around 800 °C, 5-hour air exposure) while preserving the inherent room-temperature and high-temperature mechanical properties of the cast alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Al concentration within the 2–5 at.% range that maximizes oxidation resistance without adversely affecting mechanical properties requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another set with an additional 3 at.% Al, produced under identical casting conditions. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM/EDS and XRD) to assess the continuity and composition of the oxide scales, and compare mass gains. Additionally, measure room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength to ensure mechanical performance is preserved.
measurements: Mass gain and oxide scale thickness (for oxidation resistance)
SEM/EDS and XRD analysis of the oxide layer (to confirm formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale)
High-temperature (around 1000 °C) mechanical testing (to evaluate yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the Al-alloyed samples do not exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate (i.e., similar or greater mass gain/oxide scale degradation compared to undoped samples) or if the introduction of Al leads to a meaningful deterioration in room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.

cited_evidence.text: The development of oxidation resistance in an alloy requires the presence of an alloying addition that oxidises selectively to produce a protective oxide. The latter requires the oxide to be more stable than that of the base metal. Therefore, a necessary but not sufficient requirement for the formation of a protective oxide on the surface on an alloy is that the oxide is more stable than all possible oxides. Al2O3 and SiO2 are highly stable oxides owing to their low standard free energies of formation and are desirable for oxidation protection at T > 1000 °C. In terms of the standard free energy of oxide formation, the oxides of Nb and Ti are nearly as stable as Al2O3 and SiO2. Which oxide is stable on an alloy also depends on metal activities. Changes in the activities of the elements of an alloy can change the composition of oxidation products significantly. For the oxide of an element to form, the latter must be available at the oxide/alloy or alloy/gas interface and the partial pressure of oxygen in contact with the alloy must exceed the equilibrium pressure for the oxidising reaction at that value of the activity of the element. Data for parabolic rate constants of various oxides demonstrates the superiority of Al2O3 and SiO2 scales over other oxides []. Al2O3 and SiO2 are highly stable and exhibit low diffusivities for cations and anions. Al2O3 has small deviations from stoichiometry, low point defect concentrations, and high melting point (2050 °C). SiO2 is more permeable to oxygen and nitrogen than alumina at high temperature and has a lower melting temperature []. The activation energy for diffusion of oxygen in silica is lower than in alumina. Thus, alumina becomes less effective oxidation barrier than silica as temperature is increased. Nevertheless, Al2O3 is an excellent barrier to penetration by oxygen and grows at a slower rate than silica at temperatures to about 1300 °C. Alumina and/or SiO2 scales would be desirable to form on Nb-silicide based alloys. The activity of Al required for the formation of Al2O3 cannot be provided by the Al concentration in the Nb-silicide based alloys owing to the effect of the latter on mechanical behaviour at low and high temperatures. Formation of SiO2 is more likely but depends on alloy microstructure and the formation of Nb2O5 on the scale (see below).

Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
